results.content: # Function Parameters in Detail. This time we’ll look at function arguments and parameters. In this post, we’ll cover everything from function overloading to default arguments and parameter destructuring. An argument is something we pass into a function, while parameters are something a function has. When invoking a function we give it values as arguments, but when we access the values again they’re parameters. In JavaScript, trailing commas are legal in arguments and parameters (`function fn1(a, b,) {}` and `fn1(1, 2,);`), but only in the most modern browsers as it's part of the newest language specifications. Function overloading is the act of defining multiple functions/methods with the same name but different parameter lists, and making the language chose what function to use based on arguments when invoking. function logAll(/* no explicit parameters */) { for (let i of arguments) { console.log(i); }}logAll(1, 2, 3, 4);//=> 1//=> 2//=> 3//=> 4. We see there are no parameters to the function `logAll`, but there are four arguments. function logEven(/* no explicit parameters */) { const even = arguments.filter(i => i % 2 === 0); for (let i of even) { console.log(i); }}logEven(1, 2, 3, 4);// TypeError: arguments.filter is not a function. function logEven(/* no explicit parameters */) { const even = Array.from(arguments).filter(i => i % 2 === 0); for (let i of even) { console.log(i); }}logEven(1, 2, 3, 4);//=> 2//=> 4. When talking about function arguments and parameters, we often talk about function length. function logAll(/* no explicit parameters */) { for (let i of arguments) console.log(i);}console.log(logAll.length); //=> 0. results.content:
Title: What media query breakpoints should you use? (2021) - Coder Coder
# What media query breakpoints should you use? When you’re building a responsive website, it can be confusing to know exactly how to write media queries, and which breakpoints are good to should use. Should you use `min-width` or `max-width` in your media queries? Media queries are a type of CSS at-rule which we can use to target specific conditions for sets of CSS styles. In responsive design, we usually use device widths as the criteria when writing media queries. h1 { font-size: 3rem; } @media (min-width: 43em){ h1 { font-size: 3.75rem; } }. We’re targeting a range of widths by using `min-width`in the media feature rule, so that any viewport at 43em (688px) or greater will meet the criteria. In responsive design, the widths that we target in our media queries are called breakpoints, because that is the point at which we will change the CSS rules. You might add on additional media queries to continue changing the `h1` size as the viewport increases to 62em (992px) and 87em (1392px) wide. So then, how many breakpoints should you use in your media queries? Here’s one rule of thumb– don’t try to create tons of media queries with breakpoints targeting every device width that exists. ### Should you use min-width or max-width in your breakpoints? One common question I see a lot is if you should use `min-width`, `max-width`, or both in your media query breakpoints. Then you add styles for progressively larger devices using min-width media queries. We can do this in CSS by creating a media query with a criteria of 62em (992px) that will take effect starting at smaller desktop widths. Now, what if instead we wanted to use `max-width` media queries? It takes a bit of math to calculate it out, but again, once you’ve determined which breakpoint widths you will be using, you can reuse them for all your media queries. This is an issue with accessibility, and so it’s generally not a great solution to use pixels for important measurements like `font-size` and breakpoint widths. I hope this article has helped explain what breakpoints you should use in your media queries!

results.content: # What responsive breakpoints should we build for? Optimal responsive breakpoints for designing websites are 360px for mobile, 768px for tablets, and 1366px for desktops, and these choices are based on device market share, viewport statistics, and design considerations. The question we try to evaluate regularly is **“What are the appropriate responsive breakpoints given the rapidly evolving landscape of phones, tablets, laptops and desktops?”** It is common practice to design sites for three responsive breakpoints: mobile, tablet and desktop — for reasons of time and budget. So, if we are constrained to looking at three responsive breakpoints, what should they be and how does one go about deciding? Considering the iPhone device distribution below, it is safe to say that designing for the iPhone 6 and beyond captures 80% of the market. And if we look at the viewport sizes for iPhone 6 and above, it is easy to decide that the lowest size should be 375px.
